parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's day of work and news
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer rises angry with his boy for lying late in bed and forgetting his lute. After a morning at the office and dinner, he goes to Gresham College, where he takes pleasure in hearing Commissioner Pett and Mr. Castle discuss a ship's draught. He works late at the office to his content, though he notes the struggle to settle at home or stay in once there. In the evening a letter from Plymouth tells him two ships were lost aground and a Dutch fleet is heading there, which he calls most sad news, and on coming home he is troubled to hear his canary bird of three or four years is dead.

parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's workday and news
parsed.narrative.summary: The subject begins the day angry with his boy for lying late in bed and forgetting his lute. He works at the office, goes to the Exchange, and after dinner meets Lord Brunker, Commissioner Pett and Mr. Castle at Gresham College, where he takes great pleasure in hearing them discuss a ship's draught. Late at his office he does business to his content, though he notes his difficulty in settling to work at home. In the evening a letter from Plymouth reports two ships lost aground and a Dutch fleet approaching, which he calls most sad news, and on coming home he is much troubled to hear his canary bird of three or four years is dead.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Povy's blundering
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist walked to Mr. Povy's by appointment, then went with him to Lord Ashley's, where Povy confounded himself and his business with many words and no understanding. They broke up dissatisfied and referred the matter to a later meeting. He found it strange to sit in Committee with his hat on while Mr. Sherwin stood bare, but he thanked God he thought himself no better a man for it. He dined merrily on pheasants, joked about Povy's folly, worked late at the office, sorted his books and went to bed hoping the frost would break.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Povy's accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist spent the morning directing the rebinding of many old books at his bookseller's. He dined with Lady Sandwich, undertook to convey her letter to Lord Sandwich at Portsmouth, and she raised suspicions that Creed was a fanatic and a false fellow. He replied that Creed was shrewd and cunning, and she agreed. parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went by coach through a great thaw to Mr. Povy's, where they agreed an answer to the Lords, then to Exeter House where a witness was angrily rebuked for a foolish claim about the L26,000 account. He rode home with Lord Barkeley, who seems to view Mr. Coventry as an enemy, then worked at the office until bed. He notes pain from the weather change, great sleepiness, his cousin Percivall Angier's burial, and news of Dr. Tom Pepys's death, for which he is little sorry.

parsed.narrative.subject: naval war worries
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys describes a busy day of office work, dining with Mr. Povy, trying to see the Duke of Albemarle, buying bands from his new seamstress, and finding his house neat. He notes the arrival of the French ambassadors incognito and the belief they seek an alliance against Flanders and Holland. He observes that the fleet waits at Harwich and says England could not fit out another fleet if this one were worsted, so he cries for peace. On the Lord's day he goes to church with his wife in her new gown, then walks in the garden and eats merrily with Lady Pen and her daughter.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist goes to Westminster and is cruelly vexed at being put upon uncertain errands about ships for Tangier. After dinner at a tavern and an afternoon at the office, his wife calls him to say Jane must be put away; he hears both sides and finds his wife much at fault because of her fondness for Tom, and high words follow. That night he makes himself debtor to Mr. Povy for the L117 5s. gained the month before, to ease his mind, and reflects that a quiet mind is worth all. He thanks the Lord for what he has, now L1257, and stays up over his accounts until almost two.
parsed.narrative.meaning: A quiet mind and being sure of his own is worth all.

Captain Cooke complains about the boy Tom's neglected singing and lute, and he answers him. He dines about the hemp business, and a meeting with the King and Lord Chancellor on navy debts fails. He rides in the Park with Lord Brunkard, finds it dusty, and ends the day with Mr. Warren proposing he get L100 for a ship's protection, which he thinks he will do, before supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's daily business and the Dutch war
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends a busy day at the office, dines with Mr. Povy, tries and fails to see the Duke of Albemarle, buys bands from his new seamstress and finds his house neat. He records that French ambassadors have arrived incognito and that the fleet waits at Harwich while the Dutch are not yet out. He states that England cannot fit out another fleet if this one is worsted, and he cries for God to send peace. On Sunday he goes to church with his wife in her new gown, and in the evening walks in the garden and eats merrily with Lady Pen and her daughter.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier committee and Navy funding
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attended a Tangier committee where Lord Ashley, vexed with Povy's accounts, proposed that Povy remain Treasurer until the accounts were made up; Pepys deflected the discussion and thought he had set it right, but it troubled him all day and night. In the afternoon he and others gave the Lord Treasurer, the Chancellor and the Duke of Albemarle an account of the Navy's charge and want of money, and received only despairing questions and no answer. He went home vexed, then joined Lady Batten's company where Lady Pen flung him on the bed and they were merry. He brought his wife and Lady Pen to supper, merry though still vexed, and went to bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys goes early to Mr. Povy, wanting to end his trouble of mind over the Tangier business, and offers to let Povy resume the treasurer's post, which Povy refuses. Creed then makes him doubt this, and gives reasons he finds hard to withstand, along with advice. Pepys gets Lord Barkeley and some Commissioners to order Povy to pay his remaining accounts to him, which should stop the matter being fastened on him. He dines with Creed, spends the afternoon at White Hall, takes his wife to Mile-End Green and goes home to bed. That morning he hears news that the fleets were engaged and Captain Teddiman lost his legs, but by night learns it was false and is heartily glad.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier Privy Seal
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rose at five and went to Chelsea, where, after fearing difficulties, Lord Privy Seal passed his Tangier Privy Seal at first reading and was civil to him. He returned to London very joyed, told Povy, and enjoyed a pleasant dinner at Trinity House and then saw poison experiments at Gresham College. Povy then discouraged him about getting money and suggested Backewell might scheme to take the matter over, which put Pepys into a cruel melancholy. After consulting with Creed and meeting Warren, whose help he feared would fail, he went home with a headache, hoping the next day or two would show the worst.

parsed.narrative.subject: lending money to Andrews
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator spent the morning busy at the office and dined at noon with Mr. Povy. Povy's boldness with Mercer made both her and the narrator blush. After dinner Creed and Andrews came, and the talk was mainly of Andrews's want of money. Relying on Creed's judgement, the narrator resolved to lend him 400 or 500 pounds on the security of some Tallys, though beginning this went against his heart. He worked late, went home to supper and bed, and was told of the first play at Whitehall, which he wanted to see but could not.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys speaks seriously to his boy's lute-master and says he will dismiss the boy if he neglects his lute and singing, then works busily at the office and receives news that the fleet has sailed toward Holland. On the Lord's day he takes his wife to Whitehall Chapel by Mr. Povy's coach, chats with a modest maid at a tavern, and hears Stillingfleet's sermon, which he calls the plainest and best he ever heard. He dines at Povy's, where he finds Povy's over-praising nauseating, then rides out with Creed and his wife. At home there is good music and a disagreement with Captain Taylor over a corant, which ends with everyone parting friends and Creed and Pepys laughing before bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist speaks seriously to his boy's lute-master and warns the boy he will be turned away if he neglects his lute and singing. He spends a busy day at the office and receives news that the fleet has sailed toward Holland. In the evening friends come to his house for music, he argues with Captain Taylor over a corant until Taylor is vexed, and they part friends.

parsed.narrative.subject: Sir Thomas Viner's funeral day
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist works at the office, then dines at home with Creed and puts on his new silk camelott suit, the best he has ever worn. They go to Goldsmiths' Hall for Sir Thomas Viner's burial, find it crowded, choose silk for a plain suit, and watch the large funeral from a balcony in Cornhill. Afterwards he takes a coach with a woman he calls the fairest flower to Tothill Fields, eats a cake, and does as much as was safe. He goes home to write few letters, his pleasure making him forget everything, and goes to bed after news that the fleet is in sight of the Dutch ships.

parsed.narrative.subject: month's accounts and work
parsed.narrative.summary: On the evening of 29 April the narrator finished a busy day, got the Lord Treasurer's signature on a warrant, and was troubled that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes noticed his absences from the office. He also fell asleep while writing to Mr. Coventry and blotted the letter, hoping not to offend him. On the 30th he spent the Lord's day making up his monthly accounts, found them accurate within 10s., and joyfully found himself worth over L1400. He enjoyed the modest visit and discourse of Mr. Spong, then ended the month content with his estate but troubled about Tangier and fearful of the plague and the war.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Hater's bail
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist went to Whitehall with Sir G. Carteret to secure Mr. Hater's release on bail, enlisting Mr. Hunt as second surety and waiting all morning, which vexed him as he had been kept from the office. That day guns were heard on the river as the two fleets engaged, and all hearts were full of concern for the Duke, Lord Sandwich and Mr. Coventry. On Sunday he settled his accounts, blessed God to find himself worth L1400, more than ever before, and finished his Tangier accounts with great joy. News came that the fleet was pursuing the Dutch.

parsed.narrative.subject: a busy day at the Navy Office
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist woke before 4 with great pain in urinating, which he attributes to a cold drink before bed, then slept again and went to the office. After a dinner at Sir G. Carteret's where the Board feared fresh news of the fleet, but the report of victory over the Dutch seemed written so simply that they made mirth of it. parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist describes a busy, very hot day of work on Sir G. Carteret's accounts, a merry dinner at the Dolphin Tavern, an errand to find money for the fleet, and a pleasant walk at Spring Garden. Throughout the day he and his companions are ill at ease because there is no news of the fleet or Lord Sandwich, and false reports say he was killed. He returns home weary from walking and the heat, and waits in the garden until midnight for his wife, then despairs of her coming and goes to bed. On the same day he saw houses in Drury Lane marked with a red cross, a sad sight, the first he remembered seeing, which left him uneasy about his own smell until roll-tobacco took away the apprehension.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys lay long in bed with an aching head from too many thoughts the night before. He went to Whitehall on Tangier business and met Mr. Moore, who eased his trouble by reporting the King said Lord Sandwich had done nobly. He heard of Lord Falmouth's death and the King's trouble over it. Out of joy at the victory over the Dutch he bought a coloured silk suit, then hosted a venison pasty supper with guests in place of his stone-feast. He went to bed glad it was over.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist put on a new suit that his wife said became him nobly, worked at the office, and wore his first laced band to dinner at Kate Joyce's with his mother, wife and friends. Afterwards he bought two more lace bands at the Old Exchange, then went to Deptford and Woolwich, where he discussed bringing his wife to stay at Mr. Sheldon's house for a month or two. He returned late, wrote letters and went to bed. He also noted the newsbook's favourable report of Lord Sandwich's victory and that plague deaths had risen to 112 from 43 the week before, with people growing afraid.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys works at the office until he learns the Duke of York has come and wants them to attend him. At White Hall he kisses the Duke's hands and waits all afternoon among the sunburnt courtiers returned from sea. He then goes home to the office and later to supper and bed, his wife and mother still out at W. Hewer's chamber.

parsed.narrative.subject: new clothes and daily affairs
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rises and puts on a new suit that his wife says becomes him nobly. He works at the office, then wears his first laced band to dinner at Kate Joyce's with his mother, wife and many friends. With his wife and Mercer he buys two more lace bands at the Old Exchange, then goes to Deptford and Woolwich, where Mr. Sheldon approves of his wife staying at his house for a month or two. He ends the day with letters, supper and bed, noting good news of Lord Sandwich's victory and that plague deaths in the town have risen to 112 from 43.

parsed.narrative.subject: thanksgiving day routine
parsed.narrative.summary: On the thanksgiving day for victory over the Dutch, the diarist worked alone at the office, then heard a poor sermon at church. He dined with Navy officers and Ordnance Commissioners at the Dolphin Tavern, with music at his direction, and the club bill came to 34s. a man. Afterward he went to Whitehall, then Fox-hall, where he walked alone watching citizens, and returned to his office late while his wife and mother were out on the water. At day's end he noted plague deaths at Westminster and news that the Dutch fleet had put out again.

parsed.narrative.subject: Duke of York's return
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist worked at the office until he learned the Duke of York had arrived and summoned them to attend him. He went to Whitehall, kissed the Duke's hands and waited all afternoon among the returned courtiers. Seeing Mr. Coventry rejoiced his heart, and the two walked apart to discuss the naval battle, including who served well and who did badly. He then went home to his office, supper and bed, noting his wife and mother were out at W. Hewer's chamber.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist worked at the office until he learned the Duke of York had arrived and wanted them to attend him. He went to Whitehall, kissed the Duke's hands and waited all afternoon, then met Mr. Coventry, which rejoiced his heart. He then returned to the office and went home to supper and bed, his wife and mother still out.

He dined with the Navy officers and the Ordnance Commissioners at the Dolphin Tavern, with music at his direction, and the club bill came to 34s. a man. He noted that four or five died of plague in Bell Alley at Westminster, though people expected fewer deaths, and that the Dutch fleet had come out again.

parsed.narrative.subject: plague-time workday
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist goes by water to Whitehall, where the Court is packing to leave town because of the plague. He drinks at the Harp and Ball and talks with Mary, who mentions living at his neighbour's, so he stops the conversation. He notes the plague worsening in his end of town, though only four deaths in the City, which he calls a great blessing. He does Tangier business, takes leave of Mr. Coventry, dines merrily with Mrs. Hunt, works at the office until 10, and resolves to try keeping daylight hours for a month.

He finished his letters at the office and spent a merry evening with W. Pen talking of travels before bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's workday and the cancelled book
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys wakes and talks with his wife about a letter; she satisfies him that she does not know its source, and he lets the matter pass and they are friends again. He spends the day on navy business with Lord Brouncker, resolving the shipwrights' desertion over lack of money, and dines with company. In the evening they demand a book of Rates from a clerk and, against Pepys's will, cancel the finished part, which vexes the clerk's mistress. After company leaves he walks in the fields with his wife and household, sings and goes to bed. He says he was in great trouble all day over his boy Tom, who returned that night from Greenwich for fear of the plague.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys woke and talked with his wife about a letter; she said she did not know its source, and he chose to let it pass so as not to vex himself in a strange place at a melancholy time. He spent the day on navy business with Lord Bruncker, looking into the Shipwrights' desertion from work over lack of money, and reached a fairly good resolution. In the evening they demanded a neat book of Rates from Mr. Ackeworth's Dutch clerk, and he and Bruncker cancelled the finished part, which vexed the mistress, who showed malicious rancour. Afterwards he walked in the fields with his wife and household, sang, and went to bed. He had been in great trouble all day over his boy Tom, who went to Greenwich for fear of the plague and came home that night.

parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's workday and anxieties
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys woke and talked with his wife about a letter; she said she did not know its source and suspected her cousin Franke Moore, and he chose to let it pass and they were friends. He spent the day on office business with Lord Bruncker, looking into the shipwrights' desertion over lack of money, and believed they would return to work the next day. In the evening they made a Dutch clerk's copy of a book of Rates and ships be handed over, and cancelled the finished part, which vexed the clerk's mistress. After the company left he walked in the fields with his wife and people, then went home, sang and went to bed. He had been in great trouble all day about his boy Tom, who had gone to Greenwich for fear of the plague, until Tom came home that night.

parsed.narrative.subject: Cocke's sick boy
parsed.narrative.summary: Arriving at Greenwich at dawn, sleepy and cold, the narrator and Captain Cocke learn that Cocke's boy Jacke has gone to bed sick, complaining mostly of his head, which is a bad sign, and they fall into much trouble. The narrator hides his fear and goes to bed, then is woken at 10 with news that the boy is well, which he hears with great joy. The day passes with little office business, a delayed dinner at Lord Bruncker's, and cards at Sir J. Minnes's, where a quarrel breaks out between Minnes and the Battens. Because of the disorder and the boy's illness, the narrator has to seek lodging and sleeps well in W. Hewer's fine room in the town.

parsed.narrative.subject: silk bargain and night journey
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist reaches the fleet and agrees a £5,000 bargain for Lord Sandwich with Sir Roger Cuttance, nearly signing for the whole sum but escaping it by chance, and later is glad given doubts about Captain Cocke. After dinner with Sir W. Pen, a silk bargain is made and Lord Sandwich is spoken to about trusting Cocke. Travelling toward Chatham by wherry in the dark, the party is vexed by a lost waterman and an unresponsive fisher boy, and is surprised by the fiery look of the sea-water. They reach the Crowne Inn at Rochester, make merry over the boy's seven years without a bed, and go to bed in their clothes.

parsed.narrative.subject: bargain for Lord Sandwich
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys and his party came to the fleet and aboard the Prince, where they agreed a £5,000 bargain with Sir Roger Cuttance for Lord Sandwich for silk, cinnamon, nutmeg and indigo. He was nearly signed to pay the whole sum but escaped by chance, and on second thoughts was glad, given Captain Cocke's craft. After dinner with Sir W. Pen and a talk with my Lord, they set off by wherry toward Chatham, got lost in the dark and were vexed by their waterman and an odd fisher boy. parsed.narrative.subject: end of month contentment
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the day at the office, burdened by sick and discharged prisoners left unprovided for, and dines merrily at Colonel Cleggat's. He reluctantly accepts twenty gold pieces from Luellin and gives the waiting poor men good words and a little money. Arriving at Woolwich in the evening, he finds his wife upset over a quarrel with her maids, and Mary's hint of something that would silence her stirs his jealousy. He leaves angrily, then returns, resolves to smooth the matter over and sleeps content. He ends the month with great contentment, calling the last three months the best of his life apart from the plague, and praises God.
parsed.narrative.meaning: It is not a time to put away servants, so better to salve up the business than stir it.

parsed.narrative.subject: wife's move to London
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rises and talks with his wife, who is resolved to go to London for good that day; they agree on payments to Mr. Sheldon and Mrs. Barbary. He goes to the office and is very busy having Mr. Poynter copy out his previous night's work, which pleases him. He nonetheless feels out of confidence about it after Gibson's discourse and fears it was done sillily, and he suspects Poynter's and Hater's approval may be flattery, conscious of his ignorance. He dines with his wife, takes leave of her, and works at the office until past one in the morning.

parsed.narrative.subject: a Lord's day in London
parsed.narrative.summary: On a Sunday he went to church, intending to sit near Sir James Bunce to hear his daughter and her husband sing, but was invited into Coll. Cleggatt's pew instead. After a good sermon he dined at Captain Cocke's with Colonel Wyndham, who talked of affairs of state and Lord Barkeley. In the afternoon he helped Mrs. Owen with a discharge and heard Mrs. Pierce's tale of thwarting Captain Fisher over her husband's goods. That night he fetched Mrs. Pierce again, supped merrily, walked her home, and admired her witty young boy before bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: evening of music
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rose early on a fast-day and went by water to the Duke of Albemarle, who was brisk, kind and sought his advice, and who surprised him with news that Lord Sandwich would go as Ambassador to Spain, which pleased him greatly. He spent the afternoon setting a song and then walked with his wife and Mercer to Mrs. Pierce's, where a company met to make music. He found it the best musical company he had ever been in and spent the night almost in ecstasy, wishing he could live and die in it. Mr. Pierce then reported that the King had shown Lord Sandwich full favour, and they all went home to bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: On the Lord's day the narrator went to church, was invited into Coll. Cleggatt's pew instead of sitting where he intended, and heard a good sermon. He dined at Captain Cocke's with Colonel Wyndham, who talked of state matters and the quarrels of Lord Barkeley and others over the King's removal to the Isle of Wight. Afterwards he did a favour for Mrs. Owen and heard Mrs. Pierce tell how she saved her husband's goods from Captain Fisher. In the evening he fetched Mrs. Pierce again, supped merrily, though the hoped-for singers failed to come, admired her witty little boy, and went to bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Lord's day social round
parsed.narrative.summary: On the Lord's day the diarist went to church, hoping to sit with Sir James Bunce to hear singing, but was invited into Colonel Cleggatt's pew instead. After a good sermon he dined at Captain Cocke's with Colonel Wyndham, who talked of affairs of state and Lord Berkeley. Mrs. Owen and Mrs. Pierce came to him on business, and Mrs. Pierce told how she got her husband's goods away before Captain Fisher could seize them. In the evening he fetched Mrs. Pierce again by coach, supped merrily, walked her home, and went to bed, admiring her little boy's wit.

parsed.narrative.subject: evening of music
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator rose early on a fast-day and went by water to the Duke of Albemarle, who was brisk, kind and sought his advice, and who told him Lord Sandwich was to go as Ambassador to Spain, which pleased him. parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rose early, finished his journal and met Lord Brouncker, where he obtained a bill of imprest from Captain Cocke, to his great content. He dined with Sheriff Hooker, then met Cocke, who gave him a £2,000 bill of imprest, which gladdened his heart, and arranged an insurance scheme with Sir W. Warren. He was troubled that his parish had six plague deaths, but he concluded the insurance with Lord Brouncker and went home to bed with his mind in great rest.

Minnes's, then writes letters late at the office and goes home to bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: dinner at Captain Cocke's
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist spends the morning at the office, then dines at Captain Cocke's with colleagues; the food is partly unroasted because everyone is frost-bitten, but the company is merry and Mr. Evelyn is in good humour. In the evening he returns to the office and writes letters, then goes home with his head full of business and troubled that he let his accounts slip. He makes an oath to abstain from wine until his accounts are cleared. At home he sups on little birds with the boy's sister, whose lips he enjoys, and he also records kissing Mrs. Burrows, an old acquaintance, who visited that day.

parsed.narrative.subject: a day of naval business
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rises early to consider with Lord Brouncker and fellow officers the new instructions for signing and paying bills, and recommends Poynter as clerk to the Controller. He dines merrily with Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland, then arranges tallies with Mr. Andrews and clears L210 in profit. He spends the evening watching Lord Brouncker take apart and reassemble a watch, is vexed by a snappish reply from Madam Williams and by the Duke of Albemarle's letter demanding meetings over Christmas. He finally makes up his journal for 8 or 9 days, which eases his mind, and goes to bed, hoping the frost will abate the plague.
parsed.narrative.valence_shift: burdened and vexed to satisfied and eased

parsed.narrative.subject: day of naval office business
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the morning with Lord Brouncker and fellow officers considering new instructions for signing and paying bills, and recommends Poynter as clerk to the Controller. He dines merrily with Mr. Hill and friends, then arranges tallies with Mr. Andrews, clearing L210 in profit. In the evening he watches Lord Brouncker take apart and reassemble a watch, and is pleased to learn something new. He is vexed by Madam Williams's snappish reply and by the Duke of Albemarle's letter requiring meetings through Christmas, and ends by bringing his journal up to date, easing his mind, before bed. He notes the frost and hopes for an abatement of the plague.
